claim: High-voltage-activated Ca2+ (CaV) channels adjust Ca2+ influx upon membrane depolarization.
source: High-voltage-activated Ca2+ (CaV) channels that adjust Ca2+ influx upon membrane depolarization are differentially regulated by phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) in an auxiliary CaV β subunit-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational description of CaV channels.

claim: High-voltage-activated Ca2+ (CaV) channels are differentially regulated by phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) in an auxiliary CaV β subunit-dependent manner.
source: High-voltage-activated Ca2+ (CaV) channels that adjust Ca2+ influx upon membrane depolarization are differentially regulated by phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) in an auxiliary CaV β subunit-dependent manner.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: At least two PIP2-binding sites exist in the CaV2.2 channels, including the polybasic residues at the C-terminal end of I–II loop and the binding pocket in S4II domain.
source: By engineering various α1B and β constructs in tsA-201 cells, we reported that at least two PIP2-binding sites, including the polybasic residues at the C-terminal end of I–II loop and the binding pocket in S4II domain, exist in the CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: The two PIP2-binding sites in CaV2.2 channels are distinctly engaged in the regulation of channel gating depending on the coupled CaV β2 subunits.
source: Moreover, they were distinctly engaged in the regulation of channel gating depending on the coupled CaV β2 subunits.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: The membrane-anchored β subunit abolished the PIP2 interaction of the phospholipid-binding site in the I–II loop.
source: The membrane-anchored β subunit abolished the PIP2 interaction of the phospholipid-binding site in the I–II loop, leading to lower PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The membrane-anchored β subunit leads to lower PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
source: The membrane-anchored β subunit abolished the PIP2 interaction of the phospholipid-binding site in the I–II loop, leading to lower PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the membrane-anchored β subunit effect.

claim: PIP2 interacted with the basic residues in the S4II domain of CaV2.2 channels regardless of β2 isotype.
source: By contrast, PIP2 interacted with the basic residues in the S4II domain of CaV2.2 channels regardless of β2 isotype.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The anchoring properties of CaV β2 subunits to the plasma membrane determine the biophysical states of CaV2.2 channels by regulating PIP2 coupling to the nonspecific phospholipid-binding site in the I–II loop.
source: Our data demonstrated that the anchoring properties of CaV β2 subunits to the plasma membrane determine the biophysical states of CaV2.2 channels by regulating PIP2 coupling to the nonspecific phospholipid-binding site in the I–II loop.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Voltage-gated Ca2+ (CaV) channels mediate Ca2+ influx upon membrane depolarization.
source: Voltage-gated Ca2+ (CaV) channels that mediate Ca2+ influx upon membrane depolarization contribute to various physiological events, including synaptic transmission, hormone secretion, excitation–contraction coupling, and gene transcription (Berridge et al., 2000; Catterall, 2011; Clapham, 2007; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: CaV channels contribute to various physiological events, including synaptic transmission, hormone secretion, excitation–contraction coupling, and gene transcription.
source: Voltage-gated Ca2+ (CaV) channels that mediate Ca2+ influx upon membrane depolarization contribute to various physiological events, including synaptic transmission, hormone secretion, excitation–contraction coupling, and gene transcription (Berridge et al., 2000; Catterall, 2011; Clapham, 2007; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: CaV channels can be divided into high-voltage-activated (HVA) and low-voltage-activated (LVA) channels based on their activation voltage threshold.
source: CaV channels can be divided into high-voltage-activated (HVA) and low-voltage-activated (LVA) channels based on their activation voltage threshold.
evidence: This is a standard classification in the field.

claim: The HVA Ca2+ channels consist of the CaV1 and CaV2 families.
source: The HVA Ca2+ channels, which consist of the CaV1 and CaV2 families, are multiprotein complexes with a pore-forming α1 subunit and auxiliary α2δ and β subunits.
evidence: This is a standard classification in the field.

claim: HVA Ca2+ channels are multiprotein complexes with a pore-forming α1 subunit and auxiliary α2δ and β subunits.
source: The HVA Ca2+ channels, which consist of the CaV1 and CaV2 families, are multiprotein complexes with a pore-forming α1 subunit and auxiliary α2δ and β subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HVA channel structure.

claim: PIP2 activates several types of HVA CaV channels in recombinant systems and native tissue cells.
source: Previous studies have shown that PIP2 activates several types of HVA CaV channels in recombinant systems and native tissue cells (Hille et al., 2015; Rodríguez-Menchaca et al., 2012; Suh and Hille, 2008; Wu et al., 2002; Xie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Dr-VSP is a voltage-sensing lipid phosphatase from zebrafish.
source: Dr-VSP, a voltage-sensing lipid phosphatase from zebrafish, can be used to examine the effects of PIP2 on CaV channels without the involvement of other downstream second messengers generated from Gq-coupled receptors (Murata et al., 2005; Okamura et al., 2009; Suh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dr-VSP can be used to examine the effects of PIP2 on CaV channels without the involvement of other downstream second messengers generated from Gq-coupled receptors.
source: Dr-VSP, a voltage-sensing lipid phosphatase from zebrafish, can be used to examine the effects of PIP2 on CaV channels without the involvement of other downstream second messengers generated from Gq-coupled receptors (Murata et al., 2005; Okamura et al., 2009; Suh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most HVA Ca2+ channels are suppressed by membrane PIP2 depletion without influencing LVA Ca2+ channels.
source: In vitro experiments using Dr-VSP have shown that most HVA Ca2+ channels are suppressed by membrane PIP2 depletion without influencing LVA Ca2+ channels (Jeong et al., 2016; Suh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using Dr-VSP.

claim: PIP2 induces two distinct and opposing regulatory effects on CaV2.1 channels.
source: PIP2 induces two distinct and opposing regulatory effects on CaV2.1 channels (Wu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The CaV2.1 channel protein was suggested to contain two distinct PIP2-interaction sites with different binding affinity.
source: Thus, the CaV2.1 channel protein was suggested to contain two distinct PIP2-interaction sites with different binding affinity (Wu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference from a previous study cited.

claim: Four arginine residues within the C-terminal end of the I–II loop of L-type CaV1.2 channels are involved in nonspecific phospholipid interactions.
source: A more recent study showed that four arginine residues within the C-terminal end of the I–II loop of L-type CaV1.2 channels are involved in nonspecific phospholipid interactions; therefore, the substitution of these basic residues for alanine decreases current inhibition via PIP2 breakdown and increases the open probability of CaV1.2 channels (Kaur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The substitution of four arginine residues in the I–II loop of CaV1.2 channels for alanine decreases current inhibition via PIP2 breakdown and increases the open probability of CaV1.2 channels.
source: A more recent study showed that four arginine residues within the C-terminal end of the I–II loop of L-type CaV1.2 channels are involved in nonspecific phospholipid interactions; therefore, the substitution of these basic residues for alanine decreases current inhibition via PIP2 breakdown and increases the open probability of CaV1.2 channels (Kaur et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The precise PIP2-binding sites have not been fully determined in CaV channels yet.
source: The precise PIP2-binding sites have not been fully determined in CaV channels yet.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: CaV β subunits directly bind to an α-interacting domain (AID) within the N-terminal region of the I–II loop.
source: Among the auxiliary subunits, CaV β subunits directly bind to an α-interacting domain (AID) within the N-terminal region of the I–II loop.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CaV β subunit binding.

claim: CaV β subunits play key roles in regulating membrane trafficking and fine-tuning the gating of CaV channels.
source: They play key roles in regulating membrane trafficking and fine-tuning the gating of CaV channels (Buraei and Yang, 2010; Buraei and Yang, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous reviews.

claim: A single β subunit can be divided into five distinct regions: conserved src homology-3 (SH3) and guanylate kinase (GK) domains, a flexible HOOK region connecting the two domains, and variable N- and C-terminus.
source: A single β subunit can be divided into five distinct regions: conserved src homology-3 (SH3) and guanylate kinase (GK) domains, a flexible HOOK region connecting the two domains, and variable N- and C-terminus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β subunit structure.

claim: The GK domain contains an α-binding pocket (ABP), which is a site for interaction with the AID of the I–II loop.
source: The GK domain contains an α-binding pocket (ABP), which is a site for interaction with the AID of the I–II loop (Buraei and Yang, 2010; Buraei and Yang, 2013; Chen et al., 2004; Opatowsky et al., 2004; Van Petegem et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The HOOK region is important in determining the inactivation kinetics, current density, and PIP2 regulation of CaV2.2 channels via electrostatic interaction with the plasma membrane.
source: Additionally, the HOOK region, a flexible linker composed of around 70 amino acids, is important in determining the inactivation kinetics, current density, and PIP2 regulation of CaV2.2 channels via electrostatic interaction with the plasma membrane (PM) (Miranda-Laferte et al., 2012; Park et al., 2017; Park and Suh, 2017; Richards et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Subcellular localization of the β subunits is primarily involved in the modulation of CaV channel gating, including inactivation kinetics, current density, and PIP2 sensitivity.
source: Several studies have shown that subcellular localization of the β subunits is primarily involved in the modulation of CaV channel gating, including inactivation kinetics, current density, and PIP2 sensitivity (Keum et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2015a, Kim et al., 2016; Suh et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: N-type CaV2.2 channels coexpressed with membrane-anchored β subunits, such as β2a or β2e, show relatively slower inactivation kinetics, higher current density, and lower PIP2 sensitivity than channels with the cytosolic β subunit, such as β2b, β2c, or β3.
source: For example, N-type CaV2.2 channels coexpressed with membrane-anchored β subunits, such as β2a or β2e, show relatively slower inactivation kinetics, higher current density, and lower PIP2 sensitivity than channels with the cytosolic β subunit, such as β2b, β2c, or β3 (Keum et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2015a, Kim et al., 2015b; Kim et al., 2016; Suh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The underlying mechanisms for the differential regulation of CaV2.2 channel gating depending on the subcellular localization of CaV β subunits has not been clearly resolved.
source: However, the underlying mechanisms for the differential regulation of CaV2.2 channel gating depending on the subcellular localization of CaV β subunits has not been clearly resolved.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: A bidentate model has been proposed where two palmitoyl chains of the CaV β2a subunit compete with the interaction of the two fatty acyl chains of PIP2.
source: Previous studies have proposed a bidentate model where two palmitoyl chains of the CaV β2a subunit compete with the interaction of the two fatty acyl chains of PIP2.
evidence: This is a model from previous studies.

claim: The bidentate model proposes that competition between β2a palmitoyl chains and PIP2 fatty acyl chains dislodges the PIP2 molecule from its binding site on the N-type CaV2.2 channels, decreasing the requirement for PIP2.
source: Subsequently, this dislodges the PIP2 molecule from its binding site on the N-type CaV2.2 channels, decreasing the requirement for PIP2 (Heneghan et al., 2009; Hille et al., 2015; Mitra-Ganguli et al., 2009; Roberts-Crowley and Rittenhouse, 2009).
evidence: This is part of the bidentate model from previous studies.

claim: Human CaV2.2 channels possess a PIP2-binding pocket within the S4II domain of α1B subunit.
source: Using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), Dong et al., 2021 and Gao et al., 2021 have recently shown that human CaV2.2 channels possess a PIP2-binding pocket within the S4II domain of α1B subunit.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent cryo-EM studies.

claim: PIP2 interaction to the S4II domain site is required for a minor shift of the S4II domain to the I–II loop.
source: PIP2 interaction to this site is required for a minor shift of the S4II domain to the I–II loop.
evidence: This is based on findings from recent cryo-EM studies.

claim: The functional role of the PIP2-binding site in CaV2.2 channel gating and the modulatory effects of CaV β subunits on the PIP2 interaction are yet to be defined.
source: The functional role of the PIP2-binding site in CaV2.2 channel gating and the modulatory effects of CaV β subunits on the PIP2 interaction are yet to be defined.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: The PM-anchored β2a subunit selectively disrupted PIP2 interaction with the phospholipid-binding site in the I–II loop, leading to a channel state less sensitive to Dr-VSP-induced PIP2 depletion.
source: Our results revealed that the PM-anchored β2a subunit selectively disrupted PIP2 interaction with the phospholipid-binding site in the I–II loop, leading to a channel state less sensitive to Dr-VSP-induced PIP2 depletion.
evidence: This is a key finding from the current study.

claim: The S4II-binding pocket of CaV2.2 channels interacted with PIP2 regardless of the coupled β2 isotype.
source: However, the S4II-binding pocket of CaV2.2 channels interacted with PIP2 regardless of the coupled β2 isotype.
evidence: This is a key finding from the current study.

claim: Coexpression of β2a(C3,4S) accelerated current inactivation of CaV2.2 channels.
source: Coexpression of β2a(C3,4S) accelerated current inactivation and increased the PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels, such as those with the cytosolic β2c subunit.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Coexpression of β2a(C3,4S) increased the PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
source: Coexpression of β2a(C3,4S) accelerated current inactivation and increased the PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels, such as those with the cytosolic β2c subunit.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of the chimeric Lyn-β2c slowed down the inactivation rate of CaV2.2 channels.
source: Expression of the chimeric Lyn-β2c slowed down the inactivation rate and decreased PIP2 sensitivity, like the channels with the PM-anchored β2a subunit (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of the chimeric Lyn-β2c decreased PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
source: Expression of the chimeric Lyn-β2c slowed down the inactivation rate and decreased PIP2 sensitivity, like the channels with the PM-anchored β2a subunit (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cells co-transfected with the PM-tethered chimeric Lyn-48aa-β2c showed faster current inactivation of CaV2.2 channels.
source: Interestingly, cells co-transfected with the PM-tethered chimeric Lyn-48aa-β2c showed faster current inactivation and higher PIP2 sensitivity in CaV2.2 channels, which were similar to the responses of channels with the cytosolic β2c subunit.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cells co-transfected with the PM-tethered chimeric Lyn-48aa-β2c showed higher PIP2 sensitivity in CaV2.2 channels.
source: Interestingly, cells co-transfected with the PM-tethered chimeric Lyn-48aa-β2c showed faster current inactivation and higher PIP2 sensitivity in CaV2.2 channels, which were similar to the responses of channels with the cytosolic β2c subunit.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: The N-terminal length of PM-tethering CaV β subunit is important in determining current inactivation of CaV2.2 channels.
source: Together, these data suggest that the N-terminal length of the PM-tethering CaV β subunit is critical in determining the inactivation kinetics and PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the section.

claim: The N-terminal length of PM-tethering CaV β subunit is important in determining PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
source: Together, these data suggest that the N-terminal length of the PM-tethering CaV β subunit is critical in determining the inactivation kinetics and PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the section.

claim: Disruption of the SH3–GK interaction in the membrane-anchored β2a subunit accelerates the channel inactivation of CaV2.1 channels.
source: It has been previously reported that disruption of the SH3–GK interaction in the membrane-anchored β2a subunit accelerates the channel inactivation of CaV2.1 channels (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The GK domain of the CaV β subunit interacts directly with the AID domain in the I–II loop of CaV α1 subunits.
source: The GK domain of the CaV β subunit interacts directly with the AID domain in the I–II loop of CaV α1 subunits (Buraei and Yang, 2010; Buraei and Yang, 2013; Chen et al., 2004; Opatowsky et al., 2004; Van Petegem et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Disruption of the SH3–GK interaction in the CaV β subunit may increase the length between the N-terminus and the GK–AID complex through the flexible HOOK region.
source: The GK domain of the CaV β subunit interacts directly with the AID domain in the I–II loop of CaV α1 subunits (Buraei and Yang, 2010; Buraei and Yang, 2013; Chen et al., 2004; Opatowsky et al., 2004; Van Petegem et al., 2004); therefore, disruption of the SH3–GK interaction in the CaV β subunit may increase the length between the N-terminus and the GK–AID complex through the flexible HOOK region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural knowledge of the β subunit.

claim: CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-(∆N)β2 WT exhibited slow inactivation and weak PIP2 sensitivity.
source: In contrast, CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-(∆N)β2 WT exhibited slow inactivation and weak PIP2 sensitivity.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-(∆N)β2 Mut exhibited fast inactivation and strong PIP2 sensitivity.
source: However, the channels with Lyn-(∆N)β2 Mut exhibited fast inactivation and strong PIP2 sensitivity, like channels with cytosolic (∆N)β2 WT and (∆N)β2 Mut (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The length from the N-terminal lipid anchor to the GK domain of β subunit is crucial in determining the inactivation rate of CaV2.2 channels.
source: These data suggested that the length from the N-terminal lipid anchor to the GK domain of β subunit is crucial in determining the inactivation rate and PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the section.

claim: The length from the N-terminal lipid anchor to the GK domain of β subunit is crucial in determining the PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
source: These data suggested that the length from the N-terminal lipid anchor to the GK domain of β subunit is crucial in determining the inactivation rate and PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the section.

claim: Rapamycin treatment irreversibly enhanced the FRETr signal in CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-FRB-HOOK-GK-FKBP (RF).
source: In contrast, in CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-FRB-HOOK-GK-FKBP (RF), rapamycin treatment irreversibly enhanced the FRETr signal and increased the current amplitude of CaV2.2 channels (Figure 3B, middle and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Rapamycin treatment increased the current amplitude of CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-FRB-HOOK-GK-FKBP (RF).
source: In contrast, in CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-FRB-HOOK-GK-FKBP (RF), rapamycin treatment irreversibly enhanced the FRETr signal and increased the current amplitude of CaV2.2 channels (Figure 3B, middle and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Rapamycin treatment reduced the current inactivation of CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-FRB-HOOK-GK-FKBP (RF).
source: Moreover, rapamycin treatment reduced the current inactivation and PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Rapamycin treatment reduced the PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-FRB-HOOK-GK-FKBP (RF).
source: Moreover, rapamycin treatment reduced the current inactivation and PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both the current inactivation and PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels became gradually stronger as the inserted flexible linkers became longer.
source: Our results showed that both the current inactivation and PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels became gradually stronger as the inserted flexible linkers became longer (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The current activation was gradually accelerated by the increase in linker length.
source: Consistently, the current activation was gradually accelerated by the increase in linker length (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The PIP2 sensitivity and inactivation kinetics of CaV channels were differentially regulated by the length between the lipid anchor and the GK domain.
source: Interestingly, the PIP2 sensitivity and inactivation kinetics of CaV channels were differentially regulated by the length between the lipid anchor and the GK domain: the channels with Lyn-43aa-GK showed faster inactivation than the channels with Lyn-22aa-GK, whereas the PIP2 sensitivity of the two channels was not significantly different (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The biophysical gating properties of CaV2.2 channels with a membrane-anchored β2a subunit were similar to those of channels with Lyn-9aa-GK.
source: Additionally, our data analysis indicated that the biophysical gating properties of CaV2.2 channels with a membrane-anchored β2a subunit were similar to those of channels with Lyn-9aa-GK.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis in Figure 4.

claim: The gating properties of CaV2.2 channels coupled with cytosolic β2c were similar to those of channels with Lyn-20aa-GK.
source: Furthermore, the gating properties of CaV2.2 channels coupled with cytosolic β2c were similar to those of channels with Lyn-20aa-GK (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis in Figure 4.

claim: The current density of CaV2.2 channels with β2a was significantly higher than that of channels with β2c.
source: In line with this, we found that the current density of CaV2.2 channels with β2a was significantly higher than that of channels with β2c (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: CaV2.2 channels showed slightly decreased current density that was dependent on the expansion of the flexible linker length between Lyn and the GK domain alone.
source: CaV2.2 channels showed slightly decreased current density that was dependent on the expansion of the flexible linker length between Lyn and the GK domain alone (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A, C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Voltage-dependent activation of CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-linker-GK derivatives showed a greater shift to positive voltage as the inserted flexible linkers increased in length.
source: Voltage-dependent activation of CaV2.2 channels with Lyn-linker-GK derivatives showed a greater shift to positive voltage as the inserted flexible linkers increased in length (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Incremental increases in linker length lead to a decreased voltage sensitivity.
source: This suggested that incremental increases in linker length lead to a decreased voltage sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference from the voltage-dependent activation data.

claim: Differential regulation of CaV2.2 channel gating by β subunits is mainly determined by the anchoring properties of the β subunits to PM.
source: Together, these results suggested that differential regulation of CaV2.2 channel gating by β subunits is mainly determined by the anchoring properties of the β subunits to PM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the section.

claim: A polybasic motif consisting of four basic amino acids within the C-terminal end of the I–II loop of L-type CaV1.2 channels interacts with membrane phospholipids, including PIP2.
source: Recently, Kaur et al., 2015 have reported that a polybasic motif consisting of four basic amino acids within the C-terminal end of the I–II loop of L-type CaV1.2 channels interacts with membrane phospholipids, including PIP2.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The putative PIP2-binding site is conserved in the I–II loop of N-type CaV2.2 channels.
source: Additionally, the putative PIP2-binding site is conserved in the I–II loop of N-type CaV2.2 channels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In CaV2.2 channels with the β2a subunit, the inactivation kinetics of the current did not differ between WT α1B and 4A α1B.
source: In CaV2.2 channels with the β2a subunit, the inactivation kinetics of the current did not differ between WT α1B and 4A α1B (Figure 5B, C, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: In CaV2.2 with β2c, the inactivation rate was slower in 4A α1B channels.
source: However, in CaV2.2 with β2c, the inactivation rate was slower in 4A α1B channels (Figure 5B, C, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: PIP2 depletion by Dr-VSP activation similarly inhibited the CaV current by approximately 5% in cells expressing either WT or 4A CaV2.2 channels with a PM-anchored β2a subunit.
source: By contrast, PIP2 depletion by Dr-VSP activation similarly inhibited the CaV current by approximately 5% in cells expressing either WT or 4A CaV2.2 channels with a PM-anchored β2a subunit (Figure 5E, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is another PIP2-binding site in the α1B subunit other than the polybasic motif in I–II loop.
source: By contrast, PIP2 depletion by Dr-VSP activation similarly inhibited the CaV current by approximately 5% in cells expressing either WT or 4A CaV2.2 channels with a PM-anchored β2a subunit (Figure 5E, left). This indicated the presence of another PIP2-binding site in the α1B subunit other than this polybasic motif in I–II loop.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that 4A mutation does not eliminate all PIP2 sensitivity.

claim: The PIP2 sensitivity in channels with β2c was dramatically reduced in 4A channels.
source: On the other hand, the PIP2 sensitivity in channels with β2c was dramatically reduced in 4A channels, indicating that the polybasic motif in the I–II loop plays a key role in PIP2 regulation of CaV2.2 channels with the cytosolic β subunit (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The polybasic motif in the I–II loop plays a key role in PIP2 regulation of CaV2.2 channels with the cytosolic β subunit.
source: On the other hand, the PIP2 sensitivity in channels with β2c was dramatically reduced in 4A channels, indicating that the polybasic motif in the I–II loop plays a key role in PIP2 regulation of CaV2.2 channels with the cytosolic β subunit (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Two different PIP2-interacting sites with differential PIP2 sensitivities exist in CaV2.2 channels.
source: Together, our data suggested that two different PIP2-interacting sites with differential PIP2 sensitivities exist in CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the section.

claim: PIP2 interacts with the polybasic motif when CaV2.2 is expressed with cytosolic β subunits but not when expressed with lipidated membrane-anchored β subunit.
source: More importantly, our data indicate that PIP2 interacts with the polybasic motif when CaV2.2 is expressed with cytosolic β subunits but not when expressed with lipidated membrane-anchored β subunit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the section.

claim: M1R activation inhibited the current by approximately 5% in cells expressing either α1C-1B WT or 4A channels with β2a subunit.
source: M1R activation inhibited the current by approximately 5% in cells expressing either α1C-1B WT or 4A channels with β2a subunit, which were similar to the responses of regulation by Dr-VSP-mediated PIP2 depletion in those channels (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Current suppression by M1R activation was much weaker in α1C-1B 4A channels with β2c than in α1C-1B WT with β2c.
source: However, consistent with the results for Dr-VSP-induced channel modulation, current suppression was much weaker in α1C-1B 4A channels with β2c than in α1C-1B WT with β2c (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Two basic residues (R584 and K587) within S4II domain of α1B interact with the 5-phosphate group of membrane PIP2.
source: Recently, the cryo-electron microscopic structure of human CaV2.2 complex composed of α1B, α2δ1, and β3 subunits was revealed at a resolution of 3.0 Å (Dong et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021). These studies have shown that the 5-phosphate group of membrane PIP2 interacts with two basic residues (R584 and K587) within S4II domain of α1B.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent cryo-EM studies.

claim: Mutation of the two basic residues in S4II completely abolished the Dr-VSP-mediated current inhibition in cells expressing WT α1B RA/KA or 4A α1B RA/KA with the β2a subunit.
source: Mutation of the two basic residues in S4II completely abolished the Dr-VSP-mediated current inhibition in cells expressing WT α1B RA/KA or 4A α1B RA/KA with the β2a subunit, while there was approximately 5% inhibition in cells expressing WT and 4A α1B with β2a (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: PIP2 depletion significantly inhibited the currents in cells expressing WT α1B RA/KA and β2c.
source: Importantly, PIP2 depletion significantly inhibited the currents in cells expressing WT α1B RA/KA and β2c, whereas 4A α1B RA/KA exhibited no current inhibition, like α1B RA/KA with β2a (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: The two basic residues within the S4II domain consistently interact with PIP2 regardless of the coupled β2 isotype.
source: Together, our results suggest that the two basic residues within the S4II domain consistently interact with PIP2 regardless of the coupled β2 isotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the section.

claim: PIP2-binding to the S4II-binding pocket is important in maintaining stable CaV2.2 channel gating.
source: Additionally, PIP2-binding to the S4II-binding pocket is important in maintaining stable CaV2.2 channel gating.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the section.

claim: CaV2.2 channels complexed with any β isotype can interact with membrane PIP2 through the binding pocket in the S4II domain.
source: Our data predict that CaV2.2 channels complexed with any β isotype can interact with membrane PIP2 through the binding pocket in the S4II domain (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental data.

claim: In CaV2.2 channels with cytosolic β2c, there is another interaction with PIP2 through the nonspecific phospholipid-binding site at the distal end of the α1B I–II loop.
source: However, in CaV2.2 channels with cytosolic β2c, there seems to be another interaction with PIP2 through the nonspecific phospholipid-binding site at the distal end of the α1B I–II loop.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: In channels with β2a, the membrane anchoring of the subunit may interfere with the interaction between the phospholipid-binding site and PIP2.
source: In channels with β2a, the membrane anchoring of the subunit may interfere with the interaction between the phospholipid-binding site and PIP2.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: The neutralization of polybasic residues in the I–II loop to alanine abolished PIP2 binding on the phospholipid-binding site regardless of β isotype.
source: Additionally, the neutralization of polybasic residues in the I–II loop to alanine abolished PIP2 binding on the phospholipid-binding site regardless of β isotype, which led to the less PIP2-sensitive state (Figure 8, 4A α1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The neutralization of two basic residues in the S4II-binding pocket slightly reduced PIP2 sensitivity in channels with cytosolic β2c subunits and completely abolished the response in channels with a β2a subunit.
source: By contrast, the neutralization of two basic residues in the S4II-binding pocket slightly reduced PIP2 sensitivity in channels with cytosolic β2c subunits and completely abolished the response in channels with a β2a subunit (Figure 8, α1B RA/KA).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: When PIP2 molecules were depleted at the VSDII PIP2 and polybasic phospholipid-binding sites or both sites were mutated to neutralized amino acid residues, the channels move to a nonconducting state.
source: Taken together, these data showed that when PIP2 molecules were depleted at the VSDII PIP2 and polybasic phospholipid-binding sites or both sites were mutated to neutralized amino acid residues, the channels move to a nonconducting state (Figure 8, 4A α1B RA/KA).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The hydrophobic interaction of the palmitoyl or myristoyl groups of CaV β2a or Lyn-β constructs with channel complex may be the cause of PIP2 release from the lower-affinity I–II loop phospholipid-binding site.
source: The hydrophobic interaction of the palmitoyl or myristoyl groups of CaV β2a or Lyn-β constructs with channel complex may be the cause of PIP2 release from the lower-affinity I–II loop phospholipid-binding site (Roberts-Crowley and Rittenhouse, 2009).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism with support from a citation.

claim: The PIP2 sensitivity of the CaV2.2 channel is mainly affected by the length between the lipid anchor and GK domain of the CaV β subunit.
source: This work suggests that the PIP2 sensitivity of the CaV2.2 channel is mainly affected by the length between the lipid anchor and GK domain of the CaV β subunit.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The polybasic residues in the I–II loop tether to the anionic phospholipids through the electrostatic interaction and this dipole–dipole interaction may contribute to the low-affinity phospholipid-binding site.
source: We hypothesize that the polybasic residues in the I–II loop tether to the anionic phospholipids through the electrostatic interaction and this dipole–dipole interaction may contribute to the low-affinity phospholipid-binding site (Yeon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis with support from a citation.

claim: The VSDII PIP2-binding site forms a pocket-like structure inside the S4II domain and covered by the AID domain in the cytosolic side.
source: In contrast, the VSDII PIP2-binding site forms a pocket-like structure inside the S4II domain and covered by the AID domain in the cytosolic side (Dong et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021), which could stabilize the domain in a high-affinity PIP2 interacting site.
evidence: This is based on findings from recent cryo-EM studies.

claim: The PIP2 molecule inside the VSDII PIP2-binding pocket is relatively less accessible to the degradation by phospholipase C or Dr-VSP, leading to the lower PIP2 sensitivity in CaV2.2 channels.
source: Thus, it is possible that the PIP2 molecule inside the VSDII PIP2-binding pocket is relatively less accessible to the degradation by phospholipase C or Dr-VSP, leading to the lower PIP2 sensitivity in CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural considerations.

claim: When intracellular Ca2+ is increased by depolarizing the cells or activating Gq-coupled receptors, the high intracellular Ca2+ concentration induces a dissociation of the N-terminus of the CaV β2e subunit from the PM.
source: Our recent study has reported that when intracellular Ca2+ is increased by depolarizing the cells or activating Gq-coupled receptors, the high intracellular Ca2+ concentration induces a dissociation of the N-terminus of the CaV β2e subunit from the PM.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Dissociation of the β2e subunit from the membrane increases both the inactivation kinetics and PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels.
source: This increases both the inactivation kinetics and PIP2 sensitivity of CaV2.2 channels (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The N-terminus of the β2e subunit is anchored to the PM via electrostatic interaction with the anionic phospholipids of these PM.
source: The N-terminus of the β2e subunit is anchored to the PM via electrostatic interaction with the anionic phospholipids of these PM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β2e subunit.

claim: Dissociation of the β2e subunit from the membrane leads to an interaction between the I–II loop phospholipid-binding site and PIP2, which changes the gating properties of CaV channels in physiological conditions.
source: These studies suggest that dissociation of the β2e subunit from the membrane leads to an interaction between the I–II loop phospholipid-binding site and PIP2, which changes the gating properties of CaV channels in physiological conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from previous studies.

claim: The interaction of CaV α1B with β subunits can be dynamically exchanged by other free β isoforms in intact cells.
source: The interaction of CaV α1B with β subunits can be dynamically exchanged by other free β isoforms in intact cells (Yeon et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The displacement of cytosolic β subunits by membrane-tethered β subunits on CaV channels will abolish the interaction with between PIP2 and the I–II loop phospholipid-binding site via lipid anchor of membrane-tethered β subunits, which alters the CaV channel gating properties.
source: therefore, the displacement of cytosolic β subunits by membrane-tethered β subunits on CaV channels will abolish the interaction with between PIP2 and the I–II loop phospholipid-binding site via lipid anchor of membrane-tethered β subunits, which alters the CaV channel gating properties.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings.
